newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan unveils more steps to help textile sector.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan unveils more steps to help textile sector.

text.p: Pakistan's caretaker government announced another package to help the ailing textile sector on Wednesday, reducing duties and liberalising imports of textile processing machinery, the commerce minister said.
The minister, Zubair Khan, told a news conference that Prime Minister Meraj Khalid's cabinet had approved the measures at a special meeting on Wednesday.
He said the government had slashed regulatory duty on polyester chips, used to make filament yarn, to five percent from 10 percent and liberalised machinery imports.
"The machinery, whether new or old, will be allowed (to be imported) without limit," he said, but gave no details.
He said a 10 percent regulatory duty on the import of sewing machines, knitting machines and their spare parts was being withdrawn to spur activity in the value-added sector.
"Textiles are the largest industrial sector in Pakistan -- and form over 60 percent of our exports -- and it is for this reason it is being given the highest priority," Khan said.
Last month the government withdrew a five percent customs duty on cotton imports to boost the textile sector and slashed regulatory duties on synthetic fibre imports.
The government had earlier removed a five percent excise duty on polyester fibre, and Khan said the move had reduced the price of polyester fibre by 10 percent in the domestic market.
Market analysts said on Tuesday the depressed textile stocks were showing signs of reviving in response to the earlier government relief package, designed to benefit spinners.
Floor brokers said they saw a slow but steady rise in the values of textile stocks, which comprise one-third of the total listed companies on the Karachi Stock Exchange.
The government acted after pest attacks prompted ginners to scale back estimates for the 1996/97 (July-June) cotton crop to 9.2 million 375-lb bales from an official target of 10 million.
High prices and successive crop shortfalls have led to the closure of more than 100 of Pakistan's 457 textile mills, while most of the rest are close to bankruptcy, dealers say.
